opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is that if you want agents that can really operate in the physical world, especially around people, you need them to have experienced an enormous diversity of situations. And the real world is just a really expensive and slow and sometimes unsafe place to collect that experience. You can't have a robot try something ten thousand times in someone's kitchen, and you certainly can't have it learn by making mistakes around a child or an elderly person.

Traditionally the answer has been simulation, but hand-built simulators have a ceiling. Someone has to author every environment, every object, every behavior, and you end up with a fairly narrow slice of the world that doesn't look or behave quite like reality. What's exciting about a world model like Genie 3 is that it learns the dynamics of the world from huge amounts of video, so in principle you can generate an almost unlimited variety of environments just from a text prompt. Different homes, different streets, different weather, different lighting, and crucially, other agents and people moving around in them.

And because it's interactive and consistent over time, it's not just a video you watch. An agent can take actions, see the consequences, come back to a place and find it how it left it. That's the ingredient you need for learning, to actually close the loop between acting and observing.

The people piece is especially interesting to me. Humans are the hardest part of the world to simulate by hand, because behavior is so varied and context-dependent. A generative model trained on lots of real footage has absorbed a lot of that richness implicitly. So you can imagine prompting for scenarios that are rare or safety-critical, like someone stepping out unexpectedly, or a person who needs help with a task, and letting the agent practice those over and over in a way that would be impossible to stage in reality.

Now, I'd be the first to say we're not there yet. There are limits on how long the interactions can be, how precisely you can control other characters, and the physics isn't always perfect. But the trajectory is what matters. If world models keep improving the way they have, I think they could become something like the training ground for embodied agents, an open-ended curriculum generator where the agent can keep encountering new, harder situations. That's always been the dream in open-endedness research, and this feels like the first time we have a plausible path to it at the scale of the real world.

r001.rationale: The response describes generating varied environments from video, including people moving in them, where agents can practice interacting with people. It contrasts these learned worlds with hand-built simulations that do not look or behave like reality.

r002.rationale: The response calls world models a plausible path and a potential training ground, but does not say Genie 3 may be the only way to teach agents to interact with people.

r003.rationale: It proposes practicing rare or safety-critical scenarios, such as someone stepping out unexpectedly, and says these would be impossible to stage in reality.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that gets me most excited about Genie 3 is that for the first time we have a world model that's genuinely general and genuinely interactive in real time. You can prompt it with text and get a world you can walk around in, and it stays consistent over minutes rather than seconds. And once you have that, the way I think about it is you've basically got an unlimited curriculum of environments.

If you step back and look at where the big wins in AI have come from, a lot of them came from agents being able to practice at scale. AlphaGo could play millions of games against itself because the Go simulator is perfect and free. The problem with the physical world, and with interacting with people in it, is that there's no simulator like that. Real-world data is slow and expensive to collect, and you can't just reset the world and try again. So embodied agents have always been data-starved in a way that language models haven't been.

What a model like Genie 3 offers is a learned simulator that's grounded in how the real world actually behaves, because it's trained on video of the real world. It's not a hand-coded physics engine where someone had to decide what objects exist and how they move. It's picked up the regularities from observation, including things that are really hard to program by hand: how people move, how a crowd flows, how someone reacts when you step in front of them. That matters enormously if the goal is agents that interact with humans, because humans are the hardest thing to simulate in a traditional engine.

And then the interactivity is the key piece. A world model you can only watch is a video generator. A world model you can act in is a training ground. The agent takes an action, the world responds, and the agent learns from the consequences. We've already started doing this, putting agents like SIMA into Genie worlds and giving them goals, and what you see is that the model holds up well enough for the agent to actually pursue those goals. That's the loop I care about: agents proposing things to try, the world model generating the situation, the agent learning from it, and then over time closing the gap to the real world.

There's also something I find exciting about how open-ended it is. You can type in a scenario that would be dangerous or rare or just impractical to set up in reality, and generate it. Edge cases, unusual interactions, situations you'd never want a robot to encounter for the first time in someone's home. And you can do it on demand, which means the long tail stops being the thing that kills you.

Now, I want to be honest that there's still a gap. The physics isn't perfect, the horizon is still minutes rather than hours, and the agent's actions are fairly limited today. So I don't think we're at the point of training a robot entirely in Genie and deploying it. But the trajectory from Genie 1 to Genie 2 to Genie 3 has been very steep, and I'd rather be building the learning infrastructure around a simulator that's improving at that rate than waiting for the real-world data problem to solve itself. To me that's the path: world models as the thing that finally lets embodied agents get the kind of experience that language models already take for granted.

r001.rationale: The response describes interactive Genie worlds as a training ground where agents learn from consequences, and says the worlds model people, crowds, and human reactions.

r002.rationale: It presents world models as an important path and says they address embodied agents’ data problem, but does not clearly say they may be the only way to teach agents to interact with people in the physical world.

r003.rationale: It says Genie can generate rare, dangerous, or impractical scenarios on demand, including unusual interactions and edge cases that would be difficult to obtain in reality.

astra-6.text:
I think the really exciting thing is that they give us a way to move from learning about the world to learning by interacting with it. An agent can take an action, see what happens, and then decide what to do next. That’s a very different learning experience from just watching a video or predicting the next piece of text.

If you want agents to work alongside people in the physical world, they need to adapt to situations that you can’t completely specify in advance. People behave differently, environments change, and actions have consequences. A model like Genie 3 offers the possibility of creating a much broader range of interactive situations in which to practice those skills, without every experience having to happen on a real robot.

The important caveat is that learning in a generated world doesn’t automatically mean you can do the same thing in the real world. You still have to establish that the environment captures the things that matter and that the skills transfer. But the prospect of giving agents that kind of varied, interactive experience is what makes this direction so exciting to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes interactive generated situations for practice, but does not identify visually realistic simulated worlds containing people.

r002.rationale: It calls the approach exciting, but does not say models like Genie 3 may be the only way to teach physical-world interaction.

r003.rationale: It mentions generating a broader range of interactive situations, but does not identify Genie 3 world events as a source of scenarios for which data could not otherwise be obtained.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s exciting is that they give us a way to move from learning about the world to learning by interacting with it. If you want an agent to be useful in the physical world, it needs to understand how its actions affect what happens next, and how that changes when there’s a person involved.

The challenge is that collecting all of that experience in the real world is slow and expensive. With a model like Genie 3, you can imagine generating a whole range of environments and situations where an agent can practice. You can vary the setting, vary the task, and expose it to things that you might not have thought to explicitly build into a simulator.

Now, that doesn’t mean that doing well in a generated world automatically translates into doing well in the real world. That’s a really important gap to measure. But it opens up this possibility of much richer training and evaluation, where agents can learn through experience before we ask them to interact with people in a physical environment.

r001.rationale: The response describes generated environments for agent practice and mentions situations involving people, but it does not clearly identify visually realistic simulated worlds containing people as the training environment.

r002.rationale: It calls Genie 3 a way to enable richer training, but does not say it may be the only way to teach agents to interact with people in the physical world.

r003.rationale: It says generated environments can expose agents to situations not explicitly built into a simulator, but does not identify scenarios for which data could not otherwise be obtained.
